lines.text: אי 40 איה
fem. Is. 23, 2; plur. אִיִּים, once אִיִּין Ez.
1. Pr. habitable ground, dry land, opp.
to water, the sea, rivers; see the root
no. 1. Is. 42, 15 שַׂמְתִּי נְהָרוֹת לְאִיִּים I will
make the rivers dry lands; comp. 43, 19.
50, 2. Hence
2. terra maritima, land adjacent to
the sea, sea-coast, whether on the shore
of the main land, or an island; like the
East-Indian Dvipa, which signifies both
coast and island. Spec. a) the coast,
the sea-coast, Is. 20, 6. 23, 2. 6. Ez. 27,
7 אִיֵּי אֱלִישָׁה the coast of Elishah, i. e. of
Peloponnesus or Greece. b) an island,
Jer. 47,4 אִי כַּפְתֹּר the isle of Caphtor, i. e.
Crete. אִיֵּי כִּתִּים the isles of Chittim, Ez.
27, 6. Jer. 2, 10; comp. Esth. 10, 1, where
אִיֵּי הַיָּם are put in antith. with the main
land, continent. c) Plur. אִיִּים very often
for coasts, maritime regions, espec. be-
yond sea, as in Jer. 25, 22 is added by
way of epexegesis הָאִי אֲשֶׁר בְּעֵבֶר הַיָּם.
Hence genr. of coasts and islands far
10. 12. 49, 1. 51, 5; espec. those of the
Mediterranean Ps. 72, 10. Dan. 11, 18,
which also are called more definitely
אִיֵּי הַיָּם Is. 11, 11, and אִיֵּי הַגּוֹיִם Gen.
Indian Archipelago is to be understood.
II. אִי contr. for אֱוִי (r. אָוָה II, see in
אִי I) pr. a howling, wailing cry. Hence
1. Concr. the howler, i. e. the jackal,
Arab. ابن آوى, piur. بنات آوى, son,
daughters of howling, Pers. شغال,
whence Germ. Schakal, Engl. jackal.
So called from its nocturnal cry or howl,
which resembles the scream of a child.
Damiri ap. Bochart. Hieroz. I. p. 843.
Found only in plur. אִיִּים, Is. 13, 22. 34,
2. Interj. i. q. אוֹי ah! alas! wo! c.
dat. Ecc. 10, 16. 4, 10 אִי לוֹ, which seve-
ral editt. read in one word, אִילוֹ wo to
him!
III. אִי adv. not, non, found Job 22, 30,
and in the pr. names אִי־כָבוֹד (inglorious)
Ichabod 1 Sam. 4, 21, and אִיזֶבֶל Jeze-
bel. It is much more freq. in Rabbinic,
espec. as prefixed to adjective forms
with a privative signification, like Engl.
in, un, in the same usage; and also in
Ethiopic, where ኢ is prefixed also to
verbs. It is doubtless an abridged form
from אַיִן, see r. אוּן, אִין; like the Greek
and Sanscr. a priv. from an.
אִי־כָבוֹד (inglorious) Ichabod, pr. n.
1 Sam. 4, 21. See in אִי III.
* אָיַב to be an adversary, enemy, to
any one; to persecute, to hate. The
primary idea is prob. to be sought in
breathing, blowing, puffing at or upon
any one, which is often referred to anger
and hatred, Germ. anschnauben. Kin-
dred is אָהַב, in which the idea of breath-
ing after passes over into that of desire
and love. The finite verb occurs only
once, Ex. 23, 22; but very freq. is Part.
אוֹיֵב as subst. an adversary, enemy, Gen.
22, 17. 49, 8. al. Sometimes it retains
the construction of a participle, 1 Sam.
18, 29 אוֹיֵב אֶת־דָּוִד an enemy to David.
—Fem. אוֹיֶבֶת collect. enemies, Mic. 7,
8. 10. Comp. Lehrg. p. 477.
Deriv. אִיּוֹב, and
אֵיבָה f. (contr. for אֲיֵבָה, as אֵימָה for
אֲיֵמָה) enmity, hostility, Gen. 3, 15. Num.
אֵיד m. pr. a load, burden, by which
one is oppressed, crushed; from r. אוּד
no. 2. Hence
1. misfortune, calamity, Ps. 18, 19. Job
2. destruction, ruin, Job 18, 12. 21, 17.
30, 12. אֵיד אֵל destruction from God,
אַיָּה f. (for אַוְיָה, r. אָוָה II) pr. cry, cla-
mour; hence
1. As the name of a clamorous bird
of prey, unclean, Lev. 11, 14. Deut. 14,
13; also keen-sighted, Job 28, 7. Sept.
and Vulg. sometimes vulture, sometimes
kite. The opinion of Bochart is not im-
probable, Hieroz. II. p. 193 sq. that it is
the species of falcon called by the Arabs
يُويُو yûyu, i. e. falco æsalon, called also
smirle, emerillon, Engl. merlin. Or
perhaps the Heb. word is a general term
for hawk, falcon, etc. whence in Lev.
and Deut. ll. cc. is added לְמִינָהּ.
2. Ajah, pr. n. m. a) Gen. 36, 24.
אַיֵּה i. q. אַי where? with ־ֶה parag.
as הֵנָּה from הֵן, Gen. 3, 9. 18, 9. al. Also

line_status.note: The running-head catchwords are printed unpointed: no hiriq under the alef of אי and no tsere under the alef of איה. Reading A adds vowels not present in the print.

Only four Hebrew letters are printed in the place-name (כ פ ת ר); there is no vav between the tav and resh — the holam is a single dot above the tav/resh join, so the spelling is defective כַּפְתֹּר, not plene כַּפְתּוֹר as in Reading A. Everything else (Jer. 47 ,4 with the transposed comma, אִי, the English) is identical in both readings and matches the print.

The second letter of the abbreviation after the first Arabic phrase is printed as a short dotted "i", not a tall "l" — the type reads "piur." (a printer's error or broken sort for "plur."). Both Arabic phrases (ابن آوى, بنات آوى) and their order match in A and B and in the image.

The first word shows a patach under aleph and hiriq under yod (אַיִן); the third item has only a hiriq under aleph with no point under the yod (אִין, the root entry cross-referenced alongside אוּן). Reading B swaps these pointings.

Under the yod of the second word the print shows two side-by-side dots (tsere), not qamets — the uncontracted form is אֲיֵבָה, matching the parallel אֲיֵמָה printed at the start of line 2. Reading B is correct.

Under the yod of the first word two horizontal dots (tsere) are printed, not a qamets; this matches the parallel uncontracted form אֲיֵבָה on line 1 (hataf-patah under alef, tsere under yod). Reading B is correct.
The Arabic word is printed with vowel points: a damma is visible above each yāʾ (matching the transliteration yûyu), so Reading A's pointed يُويُو is correct; Reading B drops the dammas.

The second Hebrew word carries a patach (horizontal bar) under the aleph, not a tsere (two dots), so אַי; and the paragogic ending is printed as a dash-with-segol plus he (־ֶה), not הָ with qamets. Reading B matches on both points.

The first he carries a tsere (two horizontal dots) and the nun a qamets with dagesh, giving הֵנָּה "hither" (the paragogic-he example parallel to אַיֵּה from אַי), not הִנֵּה; Reading A matches the print.
